all.leagueSummary: NET is still the knife fight in High Loft / Low Standards, with CRANK setting the pace while the gross ball-strikers keep making the adjusted leaderboard sweat. KeithK75 and Dan94 are producing the cleanest tee-to-green golf, while the middle and lower half is a demolition derby of short-game rescues, three-putts, doubles, and approaches that occasionally appear to have filed for workers’ comp. The window says reliable net scoring is available, but nobody has discovered a way to make ugly golf look less ugly.
leagueBullets: The best underlying golf belongs to the bomb-and-GIR crowd: KeithK75 and Dan94 are gaining heavily from tee to green, while CRANK is surviving a brutal tee game with elite short-game work.
Net and gross are telling different stories. CRANK’s adjustment-friendly chaos leads NET, while KeithK75 and Dan94 are producing the strongest raw ball-striking in the window.
The danger zone is obvious: short-game leaks, approach misses, and three-putts are turning otherwise playable rounds into full-blown scorecard crime scenes.

profiles.name: CRANK
profiles.profile: CRANK’s golf is a weekly hostage negotiation between the driver and the short game. The tee ball keeps wandering into dark places, the greens-in-regulation count stays modest, and then the wedges arrive wearing turnout gear to save the building. That rescue work is not cosmetic; it is the repeatable identity. There is enough putting punch to keep the thing alive, but too many bogeys and doubles still sneak through the back door. This is not pretty golf. It is effective emergency response with a driver-shaped liability.

profiles.name: KeithK75
profiles.profile: KeithK75 brings the closest thing this window has to a functioning golf operation. The driver creates room, the approaches keep finding the planet, and the birdie supply is steady enough to make pars feel like administrative paperwork. Even the ugly holes usually stay contained, which is the underrated superpower in this group. The only real complaint is that the short game occasionally forgets to clock in, but with this much tee-to-green pressure, there is less cleanup required. He is not playing survival golf; he is making everyone else audition for second place.

profiles.name: Dan94
profiles.profile: Dan94’s identity is simple: launch first, ask the golf course questions later. The tee game is consistently the engine, and the short game keeps the whole operation from becoming pure long-drive theater. When the approaches cooperate, this is frighteningly complete golf, with enough greens and birdies to turn the driver’s damage into actual pressure. The catch is that one cold iron stretch can make the scorecard look like it got dragged behind a truck. The swing brings the hammer; the approach game occasionally brings a folding chair.

profiles.name: HamSammich
profiles.profile: HamSammich is proof that a putter can keep a bad idea alive for several holes. The power is plainly there, but the fairways and greens arrive on a strict need-to-know basis, leaving the short game to clean up a mess it helped create. Putting has supplied enough rescue work to keep the file interesting, yet the doubles keep multiplying whenever contact disappears. The recent window shows a golfer who can flirt with contention through sheer stubbornness, then hand the course several extra strokes and call it character building.

profiles.name: DREADFUL
profiles.profile: DREADFUL’s current golf identity is less “one bad swing” and more “every department has joined the investigation.” The approach game leaks, the short game leaks harder, and the putter has turned three-putts into a recurring subscription. Even decent tee shots are getting buried under doubles and missed chances, so the scorecard rarely gets a chance to breathe. There have been isolated stretches where one piece behaves, but the broader pattern is damage control without the control. This is golf being played with the emergency brake firmly engaged.

profiles.name: MashedBROtato
profiles.profile: MashedBROtato can look like a complete golfer right up until the round changes genre. The tee ball is usually the healthiest part of the operation, and there is enough putting touch to make a good stretch genuinely dangerous. Then the approaches or short game start leaking, and the scorecard begins collecting doubles like loyalty points. The window is sharply mixed: flashes of full-course competence surrounded by stretches where nothing arrives on time. This is not a lack of tools. It is a recurring argument over which tool gets to sabotage the round.

profiles.name: IUDoc92
profiles.profile: IUDoc92 keeps finding enough fairways to suggest a responsible adult is operating the controls, then the rest of the bag stages a walkout. The tee-to-green numbers are underwater across the window, with approach and short-game misses leaving too much work for a putter already being asked to perform miracles. The latest appearance showed a cleaner scoring result, but the underlying ball-striking still looked more like survival than command. There is a usable foundation here; it just keeps getting abandoned somewhere between the fairway and the hole.

profiles.name: TEV_11
profiles.profile: TEV_11 has a three-appearance file that reads like two different golfers sharing one simulator bay. The tee game can create a platform, and the short game has shown signs of being useful, but the approaches have swung from playable to catastrophic. That volatility is the whole story right now: enough greens and birdies to show the route exists, paired with enough bogeys to make every decent hole feel rented. The putting is not the main villain. The irons are simply refusing to sign a long-term lease.

profiles.name: graycrum
profiles.profile: graycrum’s best recurring trait is the ability to keep a round alive after the approach game has wandered off. The tee work has been useful, the short game has repeatedly provided the bandage, and the overall ball-striking has produced flashes of a much cleaner player. The catch is that the sample is still compact and the results are mixed: one appearance looked composed, another became a bogey-and-double-bogey scavenger hunt. There is real recovery skill here, but relying on it this often is like bringing a fire extinguisher to a housewarming.

profiles.name: Leroy4522
profiles.profile: Leroy4522’s golf is being held hostage by the approach game. The tee ball has shown occasional life, and the short game is not completely abandoning the premises, but too many irons are producing weak looks and longer-than-necessary recovery missions. Putting has not been bad enough to take the blame, which is almost unfortunate because that leaves the real culprit standing in plain sight. The window is a strong trend of tee-to-green struggle, with bogeys and doubles piling up whenever the approach misses stop being merely inconvenient and become architectural.

5.leagueSummary: High Loft / Low Standards is being run through the NET leaderboard, where CRANK has built the strongest rolling-window file and the chase pack remains packed tightly behind. The underlying golf tells a messier story: Dan94 and KeithK75 are absolutely striping it gross, while CRANK keeps surviving with short-game wizardry despite ugly tee numbers and limited greens. At the other end, approach and tee-to-green damage are turning several cards into full-blown crime scenes.
leagueBullets: CRANK is winning the NET fight with short-game damage control, not pretty golf.
Dan94 and KeithK75 are the gross-ball monsters, combining elite tee-to-green work with real scoring pressure.
The bottom half is mostly battling approach and tee-to-green leaks before the putter even gets a vote.

profiles.name: CRANK
profiles.profile: CRANK’s golf is a hostage situation where the driver keeps demanding concessions and the short game pays the ransom. The tee ball is a recurring liability, the greens-in-regulation count is thin, and yet the scrambling operation keeps dragging the card back from the ditch. There is nothing remotely tidy about it: bogeys and doubles keep appearing, but the wedges and recovery shots refuse to let the round die. This is survival golf with a surprisingly functional emergency room.

profiles.name: HamSammich
profiles.profile: HamSammich brings serious heat off the tee, then spends the rest of the round trying to explain what happened to the golf ball. The power is obvious, but the fairways are optional and the tee-to-green file gets dragged down by a volatile mix of approach and short-game misses. The putter occasionally plays hero, which is useful because the penalty box is busy. When the long game behaves, this is a dangerous profile; when it doesn’t, the card looks like it was assembled during a fire drill.

profiles.name: DREADFUL
profiles.profile: DREADFUL has enough raw power to make the course nervous, but the rest of the bag keeps filing complaints. Tee-to-green play has been consistently underwater, with short game and putting turning ordinary trouble into a multi-hole disaster. The recurring signature is not one giant weakness so much as a complete refusal to stop the bleeding: doubles pile up, three-putts are regular guests, and even a respectable approach day gets mugged around the greens. The name is, frankly, supported by the evidence.

profiles.name: Dan94
profiles.profile: Dan94 is playing a different physical sport from most of the field. The driver creates instant leverage, the irons keep finding greens, and the birdie machine is always lurking somewhere nearby. The only wrinkle is that the NET results don’t fully cash the gross-golf check, with a few ugly blowups interrupting what is otherwise the cleanest all-around attack in the window. This is pressure golf built from the tee forward: give Dan94 a decent look and the course starts negotiating terms.

profiles.name: KeithK75
profiles.profile: KeithK75 owns the kind of ball-striking profile that makes range sessions look criminally productive. The approach game is the engine, the tee work supplies plenty of horsepower, and the putter has been more accomplice than suspect. The recurring blemish is that the scorecard can still spring a few bogey traps despite all that control, which is how excellent golf occasionally winds up wearing a less flattering outfit. When the full stack clicks, this is a brutally efficient way to make a course feel small.

profiles.name: IUDoc92
profiles.profile: IUDoc92 keeps finding ways to manufacture a respectable NET result from golf that looks like it was assembled during a power outage. The tee ball, approach play, short game, and putting have all taken turns leaking oil, while the three-putts and doubles keep trying to hijack the card. Still, the recovery instincts are real: enough fairways and timely saves keep the whole operation alive. This is not control golf. It is emergency management with a scorecard and a pulse.

profiles.name: MashedBROtato
profiles.profile: MashedBROtato has a bag full of usable weapons and absolutely no interest in deploying them in the same round. The tee game can create advantages, the putter occasionally catches fire, and the approach play has shown flashes of takeover mode. Then the wheels come off: missed targets, shaky short game, and a steady supply of doubles turn promising holes into mashed potatoes. The contradiction is the whole identity—there is enough upside to scare the field, but the floor keeps wearing steel-toe boots.

profiles.name: Leroy4522
profiles.profile: Leroy4522’s file is a long-running argument between the tee box and the approach area, and the irons are currently winning by losing. The driving can be serviceable, but the approach game keeps turning reasonable positions into awkward rescue missions, with limited greens and a particularly ugly proximity figure making the next shot feel like a dare. The putter has offered occasional ceasefires, yet the bogeys keep arriving in bulk. This is not a lack of effort; it is golf repeatedly choosing the worst available option.

profiles.name: graycrum
profiles.profile: In the one observed round, graycrum looked like a player who had misplaced the fairway map but found a small, angry short-game demon. The tee ball and approach work gave away ground, while recovery play was the clear bright spot and kept the card from becoming an even larger tire fire. There was enough power to create possibilities, but too much cleanup duty afterward. One round is not a personality profile, so for now the scouting report reads: dangerous around trouble, suspiciously familiar with it.

profiles.name: TEV_11
profiles.profile: In the one observed round, TEV_11’s short game was the lone department refusing to abandon the building. Everything before it—especially the approach work and broader tee-to-green game—was taking heavy damage, leaving the recovery crew to mop up a truly unreasonable amount of debris. The putter never found a rescue mission it could fully complete, and the card had no birdie oxygen. One appearance only gives us a snapshot, but this snapshot came with the smoke alarm already screaming.
